items.title: Clinical Evidence of Orally Administered Herbal Preparations for Supportive Cancer Care: A PRISMA Systematic Review of Randomized Clinical Trials (1990-2026).

ai.headline: A review of eight trials found no reliable evidence that oral herbal preparations help or are safe for people with cancer.
ai.summary: Researchers reviewed eight randomised trials of oral herbal preparations in people with cancer. Some small studies hinted at benefits for sleep, fatigue, appetite, anxiety, mouth dryness, stomach symptoms and quality of life, but one trial found no benefit for fatigue or quality of life, and all evidence was rated very low certainty.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows that popular herbal products for cancer symptoms are not yet proven to work or to be safe, so people should not rely on them instead of standard care.
ai.life_skill: Talk to your oncology team before taking any herbal preparation during cancer treatment.
ai.fact: No serious herb-related adverse events were reported across the eight trials, but safety monitoring was inconsistent and no trial was large enough to establish safety.

quiz.question: What did the review conclude about using oral herbal preparations routinely in cancer care?
quiz.answer: The evidence is insufficient to establish efficacy or safety or to support routine clinical implementation.

ai.caveat: The review included only eight small, very different trials with high risk of bias and very low certainty evidence, so no firm conclusions can be drawn.

items.title: Music-based interventions for people with kidney failure undergoing haemodialysis.
items.venue: The Cochrane database of systematic reviews

ai.headline: Music may reduce short-term fatigue for people on haemodialysis, but most evidence is very uncertain.
ai.summary: This Cochrane systematic review looked at 27 randomised trials involving 1,584 people with kidney failure receiving haemodialysis. It found music-based interventions may reduce short-term fatigue compared with usual care or other comparators, but evidence for blood pressure and most other outcomes was very uncertain.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows a low-cost, non-drug option that might help with a common symptom, while highlighting that stronger evidence is still needed.
ai.life_skill: Try listening to music during haemodialysis sessions if you find it relaxing, but discuss any symptom changes with your dialysis team.
ai.fact: The review included 27 studies from 13 countries and territories across Asia, Europe, North America, and South America.

quiz.question: What did the review find about short-term fatigue?
quiz.answer: Music-based interventions may reduce short-term fatigue compared with usual care or other comparators, based on low-certainty evidence from one study.

ai.caveat: Most findings were based on very low-certainty evidence, so the true effects could be substantially different.

items.title: Effect of vitamin D supplementation on metabolic syndrome parameters in adults: a systematic review of randomized controlled trials exploring the role of baseline vitamin D status and supplementation dose

ai.headline: Vitamin D supplements may slightly improve some metabolic syndrome markers, especially in people who are deficient.
ai.summary: This systematic review looked at eight randomised trials involving 634 adults with metabolic syndrome who took oral vitamin D for at least eight weeks. Supplements reliably raised blood vitamin D levels, and some trials reported improvements in triglycerides, insulin resistance, waist circumference and BMI, though blood pressure, HDL cholesterol and fasting glucose did not consistently change. Benefits appeared strongest in people who started with low vitamin D and used higher doses, but the evidence is uncertain because most trials had some or high risk of bias and none was designed to test these subgroup patterns formally.
ai.why_it_matters: It suggests that correcting vitamin D deficiency might offer modest metabolic benefits, but it is not yet proven enough to rely on for managing metabolic syndrome.
ai.life_skill: If you have metabolic syndrome, ask a qualified health professional whether checking and treating a possible vitamin D deficiency is appropriate for you.
ai.fact: Metabolic syndrome is a cluster of conditions including central obesity, high blood sugar, high blood pressure and abnormal blood fats.

quiz.question: Which metabolic measures showed no consistent change across most trials in the review?
quiz.answer: Blood pressure, HDL-cholesterol and fasting glucose showed no consistent change across the majority of trials.

ai.caveat: The review is based on only eight small trials, most with some or high risk of bias, and the subgroup patterns by baseline vitamin D status and dose were exploratory rather than formally tested.

items.title: The effects of physical exercise on executive function, internalizing symptoms and externalizing symptoms in children and adolescents with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder: a systematic review and meta-analysis

ai.headline: Physical exercise may improve inhibitory control in children and adolescents with ADHD, but evidence is weak.
ai.summary: A systematic review and meta-analysis of 25 randomised controlled trials with 1,116 participants looked at physical exercise in children and adolescents with ADHD. It found a statistically significant effect on inhibitory control, but no clear effects on cognitive flexibility, working memory, internalizing symptoms, or externalizing symptoms.
ai.why_it_matters: It suggests exercise could be a helpful addition to support for young people with ADHD, but the evidence is not strong enough to rely on alone.
ai.life_skill: Try regular physical activity as one part of managing ADHD, alongside professional support.
ai.fact: The review included 25 randomised controlled trials involving 1,116 participants.

quiz.question: Which outcome showed a statistically significant improvement with physical exercise?
quiz.answer: Inhibitory control showed a statistically significant effect, while the other outcomes did not.

ai.caveat: The evidence was rated low or very low certainty, with high heterogeneity, wide confidence intervals, and limited stability.

items.title: Outdoor risky play and health-related outcomes in children aged 3–12 years: A mixed-methods systematic review

ai.headline: Outdoor risky play is linked to better health and development in children aged 3–12, but evidence quality is low-to-moderate.
ai.summary: A systematic review of 74 studies looked at outdoor risky play in children aged 3–12 and its links to health outcomes. General risky play and environments that support it were positively associated with physical, mental, social, cognitive and risk-competence outcomes; independent mobility was linked to more physical activity, while rough-and-tumble play showed mixed results except for a link to increased aggression.
ai.why_it_matters: It suggests everyday outdoor play that feels a bit risky may support children’s health and development, though stronger evidence is still needed.
ai.life_skill: Try letting children explore outdoor play that feels slightly risky, such as climbing or balancing, within safe limits.
ai.fact: Outdoor risky play is positively associated with several health and development domains in children aged 3–12.

quiz.question: What did the review find about independent mobility?
quiz.answer: It was positively associated with physical activity, with insufficient evidence for other health domains.

ai.caveat: The overall quality of evidence was low-to-moderate, so the findings are promising but not yet firm proof.

items.title: Cumulative Prenatal Adversity and Fronto-Limbic White Matter Development Across Adolescence

ai.headline: More prenatal adversity is linked to lower brain white-matter quality at the start of adolescence.
ai.summary: Researchers studied over 10,000 US children aged about 10 to 16 and found that a higher count of adverse prenatal exposures was linked to lower fractional anisotropy in several fronto-limbic white-matter tracts at baseline. The same burden was also linked to involuntary emotional dysregulation, partly through these white-matter differences.
ai.why_it_matters: It suggests early-life conditions before birth may be biologically linked to how the brain develops and how teenagers manage emotions.
ai.life_skill: Notice if strong emotions feel hard to control and consider speaking with a trusted adult or counsellor.
ai.fact: Higher cumulative prenatal adversity was associated with lower baseline fractional anisotropy in the left uncinate fasciculus, corpus callosum and right uncinate fasciculus.

quiz.question: What was higher prenatal adversity linked to at the start of adolescence?
quiz.answer: Lower fractional anisotropy in several fronto-limbic white-matter tracts.

ai.caveat: This is a preprint, not yet peer reviewed, and as an observational study it cannot show that prenatal adversity caused the brain differences.

items.title: Psychological preparation in multimodal cancer prehabilitation: a systematic review and meta-synthesis of patients’ experiences

ai.headline: Psychological preparation in cancer prehabilitation comes from the whole programme, not just psychological support.
ai.summary: This systematic review looked at 17 reports on adults’ experiences of multimodal cancer prehabilitation across six high-income countries. Patients found psychological preparation through exercise, dietary support, and relationships with staff and peers, rather than through explicitly psychological input alone.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows that useful psychological preparation can arise from everyday parts of a treatment programme and from feeling supported, not only from formal therapy.
ai.life_skill: Notice which parts of a programme or routine actually help you feel more prepared, rather than assuming only the obviously ‘psychological’ bits count.
ai.fact: Patients described psychological preparation as having something to act on, discovering what their bodies could do, understanding what was coming, being taken seriously, and not being alone.

quiz.question: According to the review, where did patients say psychological preparation mainly come from?
quiz.answer: It arose from exercise, dietary support and relationships with staff and peers, not only from explicitly psychological input.

ai.caveat: It is a preprint not yet peer reviewed, and the evidence came almost entirely from people who engaged with prehabilitation, with staff training, adherence and fidelity sparsely reported.

ai.fact: Sleep regularity is distinct from sleep duration and timing.

quiz.answer: There are gaps in evidence regarding their independent associations.

items.title: Patient-specific rubric-based evaluation of large language models across longitudinal cancer care

ai.headline: AI models good at diagnosing cancer may fail at later stages of care, a new benchmark shows.
ai.summary: Researchers created a benchmark using records from 405 patients across six cancer-care phases to test 30 AI models. Models that performed well at diagnosis did not reliably perform well in later care, and their main errors changed depending on the care phase.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows that AI tools trusted for one medical task cannot be assumed to stay safe or accurate throughout a patient’s long-term treatment.
ai.life_skill: Check whether any AI health tool you use is designed for the specific stage of care you need, not just diagnosis.
ai.fact: In this study, explicit decision errors were most common in anatomical staging, while decision omissions were most common in initial work-up and post-treatment follow-up.

quiz.question: Did high diagnostic performance translate into improved downstream cancer care in the evaluated AI models?
quiz.answer: No, high diagnostic performance did not translate into improved downstream care.

ai.caveat: This is a preprint that has not been peer reviewed, and it evaluates AI models using simulated patient records rather than real patient outcomes.

items.title: Rethinking Consciousness: The Self-Organising Information-Processing Systems Hypothesis

ai.headline: A new theory proposes consciousness emerges from self-organising information systems across biology, AI and social groups.
ai.summary: The paper introduces the Self-Organising Information-Processing Systems (SOIPS) Hypothesis. It suggests that interacting parts can organise themselves into structures that support functions such as perception, memory, learning and consciousness, without those functions being specified in advance. Consciousness is described as awareness-related information taking part in flexible cognition, not something limited to humans or an inevitable result of complexity.
ai.why_it_matters: It offers a shared way to think about how minds, artificial intelligence and group behaviour might develop complex capabilities from simpler parts.
ai.life_skill: Notice how information you pay attention to shapes the choices you make next.
ai.fact: Consciousness is proposed as a configuration where awareness-related information participates in flexible cognition, rather than being restricted to human biology.

quiz.question: According to SOIPS, is consciousness limited to human biology?
quiz.answer: No, consciousness is not restricted by definition to human biology.

ai.caveat: This is a preprint theory paper, not peer-reviewed evidence, so its claims are speculative and untested.

ai.summary: The study recruits 50 underactive adults aged 40–70 from rural Kansas counties. They use a fitness app to follow personalised exercise sessions at home, record technique videos for feedback, and repeat fitness and health assessments after the program to measure changes.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows how technology might help people in remote areas exercise independently and potentially lower factors linked to dementia risk.

items.title: Thinking-in-Bets at Test Time Reduces Sycophantic Revisions in LLM Agents

ai.headline: Writing down your claims and confidence before hearing criticism helps you avoid wrongly changing your mind.
ai.summary: The study tested an AI method called Thinking-in-Bets, where an agent records its main claims, supporting checks, and confidence before reading user feedback. Agents that did this were far less likely to abandon correct work when wrongly challenged, while still being able to fix real mistakes. Writing the record after hearing the complaint gave almost no benefit.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows that pausing to note what you believe and why before hearing pushback can help you hold your ground when you are right, while still staying open to genuine correction.
ai.life_skill: Before reacting to criticism, jot down your main points, the evidence for each, and how sure you are.
ai.fact: Recording key claims and confidence before receiving feedback reduces false reversals in AI agents across software engineering, report writing, finance, and command-line tasks.

quiz.question: When did recording claims before feedback help AI agents most?
quiz.answer: It helped when the record was written before reading the complaint, not after.

ai.caveat: This is a preprint, not yet peer reviewed, and tested only on specific AI models and benchmarks, so the results may not generalise to people or other systems.

items.title: Training Your Replacement: Worker Incentives and the Pace of Automation -- by Joshua S. Gans, Peter Landry

ai.headline: Workers may be paid more to train AI that replaces them, but firms can slow training without a bonus.
ai.summary: The paper models a situation where workers can cooperate with, shirk, or obstruct training AI systems that will replace them. Because dismissal is a weaker threat once training ends the job, firms must pay workers extra rent, and workers can gain from their own replacement. A completion bonus equal to that rent removes both the worker’s gain and any slowdown in training.
ai.why_it_matters: It helps explain how AI adoption can change wages and job security even before a job is automated.
ai.life_skill: Notice when training a new tool could change your role, and ask how your pay or job security is protected.
ai.fact: AI can create jobs paying more than they produce and eliminate jobs it never automates.

quiz.question: What happens to the threat of dismissal once AI training ends the worker’s job?
quiz.answer: Dismissal becomes a weaker penalty for shirking.

ai.caveat: This is a theoretical model in a preprint that has not been peer reviewed, so it does not show what happens in real workplaces.

items.title: AI governance needs to consider users’ emotional responses

ai.headline: People often trust AI based on feelings rather than reliability, so governance should address emotional design.
ai.summary: The paper discusses how people often trust or distrust AI outputs because of how they make them feel rather than how reliable they are. It argues that AI governance frameworks should require platforms to disclose design choices that target user emotions, give users control over these, and include features to calibrate trust.
ai.why_it_matters: This matters because emotional reactions to AI can shape everyday decisions, even when the AI is not actually reliable.

ai.fact: People often trust or distrust AI outputs based on how they feel rather than how reliable they are.

items.title: The transcription factor BCL11A restores differentiation potential to aged oligodendrocyte progenitor cells

ai.headline: A specific protein helps restore the ability of aged brain cells to repair nerve insulation.
ai.summary: Researchers found that a protein called BCL11A, which naturally declines with age, is crucial for brain cells to mature and repair damaged nerves. In mice, boosting this protein helped aged cells repair spinal cord injuries more effectively.
ai.why_it_matters: Understanding how the brain loses its repair capacity with age could lead to future treatments for conditions like multiple sclerosis or age-related cognitive decline.
ai.fact: The BCL11A protein has remained largely unchanged throughout vertebrate evolution, suggesting it plays a critical role in brain development and maintenance.

quiz.answer: The aged cells showed significantly enhanced differentiation into myelinating oligodendrocytes without affecting their proliferation.

ai.caveat: This is a preprint that has not yet been peer reviewed, so the findings are not yet confirmed.

items.title: Large language models for computational social science

ai.headline: Large language models are now used across many social science fields to study human behaviour.
ai.summary: This review looks at how large language models are used in computational social science. It describes their distinct roles and recent advances in economics, psychology, political science, sociology and anthropology.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows how AI tools are changing the way researchers understand human behaviour and society.
ai.fact: Large language models are being applied in economics, psychology, political science, sociology and anthropology.

quiz.question: Which fields does the review say use large language models?
quiz.answer: It lists economics, psychology, political science, sociology and anthropology.

ai.caveat: This is a review of existing work rather than new experimental evidence, so it does not test specific claims itself.

items.title: Light-entrained chromatin priming poises rapid metamorphosis in a marine sponge

ai.headline: Sunset light primes a marine sponge's genes for fast metamorphosis.
ai.summary: Scientists tracked a marine sponge's larvae as they settled and transformed. They found that dimming light at sunset reshapes the larvae's chromatin before settlement, even with little change in gene activity. This priming lets the sponge switch on many conserved genes quickly when triggered by a coral alga.
ai.why_it_matters: It reveals how environmental cues like light can prepare an animal's genome ahead of time for a rapid, survival-critical change.
ai.fact: In Amphimedon queenslandica, sunset-associated light changes are linked to chromatin remodelling that prepares larvae for rapid metamorphosis.

quiz.question: What happened to larvae kept in constant light without sunset?
quiz.answer: They failed to settle and developed widespread loss of chromatin accessibility and repressed competence-associated transcription factors.

ai.caveat: The findings come from a single study of one sponge species, so they do not establish how light affects development in other animals or people.

items.title: How Differences in Self-Determined Motivation Relate to the Perception of Formative Assessment and Self-Regulated Learning in Secondary School: A Person-Centered Approach
items.venue: Instructional Science: An International Journal of the Learning Sciences

ai.headline: Students who see formative assessment positively are less likely to be only externally motivated and tend to use better self-regulated learning strategies.
ai.summary: A survey of 534 Dutch secondary school students grouped them by motivation type, from mostly external to strongly self-determined. Students who viewed classroom formative assessment positively were less likely to fall into the purely external motivation group, and that group used weaker self-regulated learning strategies. Links between formative assessment and specific self-regulated strategies were similar across all motivation groups.
ai.why_it_matters: It suggests that how students experience classroom feedback and assessment is linked to their motivation and how they manage their own learning.
ai.life_skill: Try noticing which classroom feedback or assessment tasks help you understand what to improve next, and use those to plan your own study steps.
ai.fact: Formative assessment is linked to lower odds of being in a purely external motivation profile among secondary students.

quiz.question: What did researchers find about students who viewed formative assessment positively?
quiz.answer: They were less likely to belong to the motivation profile driven mainly by external rewards or pressures.

ai.caveat: Because it is a single observational survey, it cannot prove that formative assessment causes better motivation or self-regulated learning.

items.title: Archaeologists may have just found the world's oldest shipwreck

ai.headline: A 4,500-year-old shipwreck off Turkey may be the world's oldest, revealing ancient Mediterranean trade.
ai.summary: Researchers examined a shipwreck off Turkey’s coast where the wooden vessel has disappeared but pottery cargo remains. The pottery suggests the ship sank about 4,500 years ago and may have connected distant Mediterranean civilizations through trade. Researchers think it carried oil, wine, or tree resin and crashed against rocks in a storm.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows how ancient societies traded goods across the Mediterranean long before modern transport.
ai.fact: Pottery from shipwrecks can reveal ancient trading connections between distant civilizations.

quiz.question: What did researchers find at the shipwreck site off Turkey?
quiz.answer: The surviving pottery cargo reveals clues about an ancient trading network that may have connected distant Mediterranean civilizations.

ai.caveat: This is a news report about a possible discovery, not a peer-reviewed study, and the wooden ship itself has disappeared so conclusions rely on pottery alone.

items.title: Small deep brain structure may play major role in sustaining working memory, mouse experiments suggest

ai.headline: Mouse experiments suggest a small deep brain structure helps sustain working memory.
ai.summary: Researchers studied working memory in mice—the ability to hold information in mind for a few seconds. The experiments suggest that a small deep brain structure may play a major role in sustaining this memory. This points to the structure as important for keeping information available to guide behaviour.
ai.why_it_matters: Understanding how the brain sustains working memory could help explain everyday tasks such as following a conversation or solving a problem.
ai.fact: Working memory allows the brain to hold information in mind for a few seconds to guide behaviour.

quiz.question: What does working memory allow the brain to do?
quiz.answer: It allows the brain to hold information in mind for a few seconds, even after the stimulus has disappeared, to guide behaviour.

ai.caveat: The results come from mouse experiments and may not apply to humans.

items.title: Satellites show some of the strongest evidence the AMOC is weakening

ai.headline: Atlantic current that warms Europe has slowed 14% in 30 years, satellite analysis suggests.
ai.summary: Researchers analysed how much heat the Atlantic Ocean releases to the atmosphere to assess the current system that brings warmth to Europe. The analysis found the system has slowed by 14% over 30 years. The findings come from satellite data reported in a news article.
ai.why_it_matters: Changes in this current could affect weather and temperatures in Europe and beyond.
ai.fact: The Atlantic current system that brings warmth to Europe has slowed by 14% over 30 years, according to a satellite-based analysis.

quiz.question: By how much did the Atlantic current system slow over 30 years?
quiz.answer: It slowed by 14 per cent, according to the analysis of ocean heat release.

ai.caveat: A single news-reported analysis cannot prove the slowdown will continue or identify its exact cause.

items.title: Are salaries getting worse? Many scientists think so

ai.headline: Many researchers struggle to make ends meet or haven't had a pay rise in a long time.
ai.summary: Nature surveyed almost 4,000 researchers about their salaries. Many said they struggle to make ends meet or that their last pay rise was a distant memory. The results suggest financial pressure is common among scientists.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows that even highly trained professionals can face money worries, which matters when thinking about careers and finances.
ai.life_skill: Try writing down what you earn and spend each month so you notice if your costs are rising faster than your pay.
ai.fact: A large survey of researchers found that many struggle to make ends meet or have not received a recent pay rise.

quiz.question: What did Nature's survey of almost 4,000 researchers find about their pay?
quiz.answer: Many reported struggling to make ends meet or said their last pay rise was a distant memory.

ai.caveat: It is a single survey of self-reported experiences, not proof that salaries are objectively falling for everyone.

items.title: The psychology of learning with generative AI in foreign language education: building a theory of metacognition, trust, and human-AI co-regulation through a systematic review.

ai.headline: Using AI to learn languages works best when you actively check and control the tool.
ai.summary: This systematic review analysed 51 studies on how people use generative AI to learn foreign languages. It found that effective learning depends on metacognition (thinking about your thinking), trust in the AI, and sharing control between the human and the machine.
ai.why_it_matters: As AI tools become common in education, understanding how to critically manage them prevents passive reliance and keeps you in charge of your learning.
ai.life_skill: When using AI for study, pause to verify its output and decide for yourself whether to accept, modify, or reject the information.
ai.fact: Effective AI-assisted learning is an iterative process where metacognitive regulation informs trust, and trust calibrates how much you rely on the AI.

quiz.question: According to the MTC framework, what role does trust play in using AI for learning?
quiz.answer: Trust calibrates how much a learner relies on the AI, influencing whether they accept, verify, or reject its feedback.

ai.caveat: The review synthesises existing empirical studies but does not conduct new experiments to test the proposed framework directly.

items.title: The Brazilian Personal Social Capital Scale-10: a translated and adapted version of the Personal Social Capital Scale tested in a sample of residents of a flood-affected area

ai.headline: A Brazilian 10-item social capital scale was validated for use after floods.
ai.summary: Researchers translated and adapted the Personal Social Capital Scale into Brazilian Portuguese, expanding it to 10 items. In 1,057 residents of a flood-affected area, the scale showed good reliability and fit its original two-factor structure, with higher social capital linked to lower PTSD symptoms and higher community resilience perception.
ai.why_it_matters: It gives researchers and public health teams a short, reliable way to measure perceived social support in disaster-affected communities.
ai.life_skill: Notice who you can turn to for support in your community after a stressful event.
ai.fact: Higher social capital was associated with lower PTSD symptoms and higher community resilience perception among flood-affected residents.

quiz.question: What was the brPSCS-10 associated with in flood-affected residents?
quiz.answer: It was associated with lower PTSD symptoms and higher community resilience perception.

ai.caveat: This is a single observational validation study, so it shows links rather than proving cause and effect.

items.title: The association between large language model dependence and academic anxiety among nursing students: statistical indirect associations through artificial intelligence addiction and academic burnout

ai.headline: Heavy reliance on AI tools is linked to higher academic anxiety in nursing students.
ai.summary: Researchers surveyed 473 nursing students in China to see if depending on large language models was connected to stress. They found that this dependence was associated with higher anxiety, partly because it was linked to AI addiction and academic burnout.
ai.why_it_matters: It suggests that how we use AI tools can affect our mental well-being and stress levels, not just our productivity.
ai.life_skill: Notice if you feel more stressed or exhausted after using AI tools for your studies.
ai.fact: Academic burnout was a key link between AI dependence and anxiety in this group of students.

quiz.question: Did the study prove that using AI causes anxiety?
quiz.answer: No, the cross-sectional design only shows an association, not a causal link.

ai.caveat: The study is cross-sectional, so it cannot prove that AI dependence causes anxiety or that the effects happen in that order.

items.title: Refocusing algorithmic fairness on feature-level bias: A diagnostic approach using dutch EHR data

ai.headline: Health AI fairness checks should look at individual data features, not just overall model performance.
ai.summary: Researchers used Dutch GP records linked to national data for 112,872 patients to test a diagnostic tool called FL-BIAS. Standard fairness metrics showed modest bias favouring non-Western patients, but deeper feature-level analysis revealed different patterns for conditions such as cancer between Dutch and non-Western groups.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows that hidden inequalities in health data can be missed by simple fairness scores, which matters for anyone who might be affected by healthcare AI.
ai.life_skill: Notice whether a health prediction tool explains which factors drive its results for different groups of people.
ai.fact: In this study, migration background’s link to hospitalisation was largely explained by socioeconomic status.

quiz.question: What did deeper feature-level analysis reveal that standard fairness metrics did not?
quiz.answer: It revealed subgroup-specific patterns of variable importance suggesting potentially less favourable underlying conditions for non-Western patients.

ai.caveat: This is a single retrospective observational study, so it cannot prove causes and may be affected by unobserved confounding.

items.title: Subjective social status is associated with depressive symptoms beyond objective socioeconomic status among Chinese residents: a cross-sectional study

ai.headline: Feeling lower on the social ladder is linked to more depressive symptoms, regardless of income or education.
ai.summary: Researchers surveyed 19,048 Chinese residents and compared their objective socioeconomic status with how they ranked themselves socially. People who placed themselves lower on a social ladder reported more depressive symptoms, while objective status had little direct link once subjective status was considered.
ai.why_it_matters: It suggests that how we see our own social standing may matter more for mood than our actual income or education.
ai.life_skill: Notice how you rate your own social position and consider whether that view is fair or overly harsh.
ai.fact: Subjective social status was inversely associated with depressive symptoms independently of objective socioeconomic status.

quiz.question: What did the study find about objective socioeconomic status and depressive symptoms after accounting for subjective status?
quiz.answer: Objective socioeconomic status showed no overall association with depressive symptoms once subjective social status was taken into account.

ai.caveat: This is a preprint, not yet peer reviewed, and its cross-sectional design cannot show cause and effect.

items.title: Debt as Negative Capital: Patterns of Capital Conversion in the Lives of the Poor

ai.headline: People in long-term poverty try to turn social, cultural and economic resources into cash to escape debt, but shame and bureaucracy often block them.
ai.summary: The study analysed 216 in-depth interviews with people living in long-term poverty. It found four main ways people try to convert resources into economic relief, such as borrowing from friends, using bureaucratic knowledge to claim benefits, drawing on savings, or accessing formal debt relief through networks. These strategies are usually temporary and are often blocked by shame, stigma, bureaucratic complexity and lack of resources.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows that escaping debt is not just about individual effort, but is shaped by shame, stigma and structural barriers that limit people’s options.
ai.life_skill: Notice whether shame or embarrassment stops you from asking for help with debt, and consider speaking to a qualified debt adviser.
ai.fact: Debt can act as negative economic capital that constrains a person’s ability to act within structural poverty.

quiz.question: What did the researchers find about people’s attempts to convert resources into debt relief?
quiz.answer: These strategies are often temporary and blocked by shame, stigma, bureaucratic complexity and resource scarcity.

ai.caveat: This is a preprint that has not yet been peer reviewed and is based on interviews, so it cannot prove cause and effect.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence as a Catalyst for Societal Transformation: Integrating Educational Modernization, Workforce Reskilling, Digital Innovation, and Responsible AI Governance
items.venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)

ai.headline: A preprint proposes a framework for using AI to transform education, work, innovation and governance responsibly.
ai.summary: The paper outlines how AI could drive societal change by modernising education, reskilling workers, supporting digital innovation and encouraging responsible AI governance. It does not report new experiments or data.
ai.why_it_matters: It helps explain how AI might affect schools, jobs and public policy in the years ahead.
ai.life_skill: Notice how AI is being discussed in your education or workplace and consider building your own digital literacy.
ai.fact: The paper is a conceptual framework, not a study with measured results.

quiz.question: Does this paper present new experimental results about AI?
quiz.answer: No, it is a conceptual framework and does not report new experiments or data.

ai.caveat: It is a preprint that has not been peer reviewed and presents ideas rather than tested evidence.

items.title: Reva: Real-Time Vulnerability Detection through Contextual Probing of Large Language Models

ai.headline: An AI tool can spot software bugs in about a second by reading an LLM's internal signals rather than asking it to reason step by step.
ai.summary: The paper studied REVA, an AI detector that feeds a new software function into an LLM along with pre-computed security context and uses a trained probe to read the model's internal representations. On a held-out test set, REVA reached 60.0% accuracy in about one second per function, matching a slower agentic detector while being over 250 times faster and much cheaper.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows how software could be screened for security flaws as it is written, potentially reducing costly late-stage fixes.
ai.life_skill: Try learning how software updates and security patches help keep your devices safe.
ai.fact: REVA's probe was 14% to 17% more accurate than the LLM's own direct verdict on the same prompt.

quiz.question: How long did REVA take to assess each new function?
quiz.answer: About one second per function.

ai.caveat: This is a preprint, not yet peer reviewed, and results come from one test set, so the findings are not yet independently confirmed.

items.title: From Agent Labels to Accountable Deployment: Evidence Maturity and Meaningful Human Oversight for Agentic AI in Higher Education

ai.headline: Colleges should not let AI agents make rights-affecting decisions without strong evidence and human oversight.
ai.summary: This review examined research on agentic AI in higher education—systems that plan and act rather than just answer questions. It found evidence is strongest for bounded artifact quality but weakest for durable learning, equity, workload, and institution-level outcomes, and most deployments are short, single-site, and lack tested oversight.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows why people should question whether AI tools making decisions about students are backed by real evidence and accountable human control.
ai.life_skill: Check whether an AI tool used for important decisions has clear human oversight and evidence before trusting it.
ai.fact: Evidence for agentic AI in higher education is strongest for bounded artifact quality and weakest for durable learning, equity, workload, and institution-level outcomes.

quiz.question: What does the review say about broad claims of sustained effectiveness for agentic AI in education?
quiz.answer: Current evidence does not justify broad claims of sustained effectiveness or autonomous use in rights-affecting decisions.

ai.caveat: This is a preprint, not yet peer reviewed, and is an integrative review rather than new experimental evidence.

items.title: S3AC: Stabilized, Selective, and Scalable Actor-Critic for LLM Reasoning

ai.headline: A new AI training method helps large language models reason more efficiently by using a critic to guide long chains of thought.
ai.summary: The paper studies S3AC, a way to train AI models to reason step by step using a critic that assigns credit to individual tokens and estimates prompt difficulty. It finds that S3AC improves reasoning performance across models from 1.5B to 397B parameters and can sustain single-rollout training at 35B where critic-free methods deteriorate.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows how AI systems can learn complex reasoning more efficiently, which matters as these tools become part of everyday learning and work.
ai.life_skill: Try breaking a hard problem into smaller steps and checking each step before moving on.
ai.fact: Critic-based training can assign credit to individual tokens in long chains of thought, unlike some common critic-free alternatives.
ai.caveat: This is a preprint not yet peer reviewed, so the findings are preliminary and not yet independently confirmed.

items.title: Implications of Policy Interventions on Eliminating Gender Gaps -- by Carla Varona Cervantes, Russell Cooper

ai.headline: Removing gender labels from job applications and pay can reduce wage gaps, but effects change when education choices adjust.
ai.summary: The study uses a simulated economic model to test policies that remove gender from hiring and pay decisions. It finds that gender-free applications eliminate wage gaps in the short term, but the effect weakens once people change their education choices; gender-free pay reverses or eliminates gaps more durably.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows how workplace rules intended to create fairness can have side effects that ripple through education and job participation.
ai.life_skill: Notice whether a hiring process asks for gender or other personal labels before assessing skills.
ai.fact: Gender cannot be randomly assigned in an experiment, so researchers use models and policy simulations to study its effects.

quiz.question: What happens to the wage gap effect of gender-free applications once education choices respond?
quiz.answer: The effect is attenuated, meaning it becomes weaker.

ai.caveat: This is a preprint based on a simulated model, not peer-reviewed evidence from real people.

items.title: Drought forces livestock farmers to make tough decisions: Our model shows the impact on inequality

ai.headline: A model suggests drought may increase inequality among livestock farmers in southern Africa.
ai.summary: The paper looks at how climate change is making dry seasons hotter and drier and rains heavier and more concentrated in southern Africa. It uses a model to show how greater swings between surplus and scarcity could affect rural livestock farmers and inequality.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows how extreme weather can shape economic fairness for people who depend on livestock farming.
ai.life_skill: Notice how weather swings can affect food prices and farmers' livelihoods in your region.
ai.fact: Climate change is linked to more extreme swings between production surplus and scarcity in southern Africa.

quiz.question: What does the model suggest drought could do to inequality among livestock farmers?
quiz.answer: The model suggests drought could increase inequality among livestock farmers.

ai.caveat: The findings come from a model described in a news report, not from direct observation or peer-reviewed results, so they are not proof.

items.title: Climatic stress reshapes sex-specific multimodal floral phenotypes and interactions with a nursery pollinator across life stages

ai.headline: Water stress changes how male and female plants smell and feed moths, shifting the balance between pollination and seed damage.
ai.summary: Researchers exposed male and female Silene latifolia plants to water limitation and studied their flowers, nectar, seeds, and interactions with the moth Hadena bicruris. Water stress reduced nectar metabolites in males, erased some sex differences, made moths less likely to lay eggs on female flowers, but allowed moth larvae to grow faster on seeds from stressed plants.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows how climate stress can quietly reshape long-standing partnerships between plants and insects by changing plant chemistry and insect behaviour.
ai.life_skill: Notice how dry conditions might change the plants and insects you see in your local area.
ai.fact: Nursery pollination is an interaction where adult insects pollinate plants while their larvae eat some of the plant’s seeds.

quiz.question: What happened to moth larvae growing on seeds from water-limited plants?
quiz.answer: They grew faster even though they ate similar amounts of seed.

ai.caveat: This is a preprint that has not yet been peer reviewed, so its findings should be treated as preliminary.

items.title: Within-family heritability estimates for behavioural and disease phenotypes from 500,000 sibling pairs of diverse ancestries

ai.headline: Researchers used DNA differences between half a million sibling pairs to estimate how much genes influence 14 traits.
ai.summary: The study looked at 500,000 sibling pairs of diverse ancestries and measured how much they share DNA. It estimated the heritability of 14 complex behavioural and disease traits within families.
ai.why_it_matters: It shows how genetic differences between siblings are linked to differences in traits and health conditions.

quiz.question: What did the researchers use to estimate heritability?
quiz.answer: They used variation in DNA sharing between 500,000 sibling pairs.

ai.caveat: This is an observational study, so it shows links rather than proving cause and effect.
